description: Conversational learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

article.title: Dark Patterns Work Too Well: Why Good Design Can Be Unethical
article.author: Emma Rodriguez

cards.title: Confirmshaming Weaponizes Guilt
cards.subtitle: Decline buttons are phrased as moral failures to make opting out feel like confessing a weakness.
body: 'No thanks, I hate saving money.' 'No, I don't want to help the planet.' The design frames your choice as a character flaw.
Guilt often converts better than persuasion. Every dismissal becomes a tiny shame event.
It's worth noticing when a design is trying to make you feel bad for saying no.
cards.takeaway: Decline options that shame you are a design choice, not an accident.

cards.title: Hidden Costs Appear at Checkout
cards.subtitle: The price was $20 for nine screens; now it's $34.50 at payment. You're too invested to quit.
body: Fees, taxes, and shipping appear at the last possible moment. You've already spent time configuring, comparing, deciding. Abandoning now feels like wasted effort.
The sunk cost fallacy is built into the flow. Transparency would reduce conversion rates, so the design deliberately exploits escalation of commitment.
Last-minute price changes are often intentional.
cards.takeaway: Hidden costs at checkout exploit the effort you've already invested.

cards.title: Unsubscribe Requires a Login You Forgot
cards.subtitle: Signing up took one click; unsubscribing needs authentication, confirmation, and explaining why you're leaving.
body: Friction-free signup, friction-heavy exit. Unsubscribing might require a password you never set.
Every barrier to exit increases retention numbers. What takes one click to join can take five steps to leave.
The asymmetry is usually intentional.
cards.takeaway: Easy in, hard out is a common design pattern.

cards.title: Pre-Checked Boxes Add Unwanted Items
cards.subtitle: You ordered a book; you also apparently ordered insurance, expedited shipping, and a newsletter.
body: Defaults are powerful. Pre-checked boxes ensure most users accept extras they didn't actively choose.
Opting out requires reading every line and unchecking. Most people don't have the time. The design bets on your inattention.
Defaults often determine behavior more than conscious choice does.
cards.takeaway: Pre-checked boxes are designed to capture inattention.

cards.title: Forced Continuity Charges After Free Trials
cards.subtitle: You signed up for a free trial, forgot to cancel, and have now paid for six months.
body: Free trials require payment info upfront. The trial ends silently. Charges begin automatically. Canceling means finding buried settings and navigating menus.
Forgetting is literally the business model for some products. Remembering to cancel is your job; reminding you isn't theirs.
Set a calendar reminder before you sign up for a free trial.
cards.takeaway: Free trials often rely on you forgetting to cancel.

cards.title: Privacy Settings Default to Maximum Sharing
cards.subtitle: Your data is shared with partners by default; opting out requires fourteen toggles across three screens.
body: Privacy controls exist, but they're buried and default to maximum sharing. Actually exercising control takes technical know-how and persistence.
Compliance with regulations isn't the same as respect for users. The design makes privacy the expensive, time-consuming option.
Default settings often favor the company, not you.
cards.takeaway: Privacy often requires active effort to protect.

cards.title: Scarcity Timers Create False Urgency
cards.subtitle: 'Three people are looking at this! Only two left!' The timer resets after every page load.
body: Artificial urgency bypasses rational deliberation. The scarcity is often fake. The pressure you feel is real.
Users make reactive decisions to avoid missing out on fabricated shortages.
When you see a countdown, it's worth asking whether it's real.
cards.takeaway: Scarcity and timers are often manufactured, not genuine.

cards.title: Infinite Scroll Removes Stopping Points
cards.subtitle: There's no end, no page two—just more content. Stopping requires willpower.
body: Pagination used to give natural exit points. Infinite scroll removes them. The next thing is always one swipe away.
Engagement metrics improve when users can't find the end. The design puts the decision to stop entirely on you.
Knowing there's no natural end can help you decide when to stop.
cards.takeaway: Infinite scroll is designed to keep you scrolling.

cards.title: Bait and Switch Changes Meaning Mid-Flow
cards.subtitle: You clicked 'Download'; the button was actually 'Start free trial and download.'
body: Button labels shift between preview and action. 'Learn more' becomes 'Subscribe and learn more.' Users click based on the initial text and miss the change.
The switch happens at the moment when you're already committed to clicking.
Hover or look closely before you click.
cards.takeaway: Button labels can change between attention and action.

cards.title: Roach Motel Lets You In, Not Out
cards.subtitle: Signing up took one click; deleting your account requires emailing support and waiting three days.
body: Entry is frictionless. Exit is deliberately obstructed. Account deletion is hidden, requires confirmations, asks for reasons, offers discounts to stay.
The design makes leaving harder than staying. Easy in, hard out is built into the structure.
Before you sign up, check how hard it is to leave.
cards.takeaway: Easy signup and hard exit is a retention strategy.

cards.title: Social Proof Can Be Fabricated
cards.subtitle: 'Join 50,000 satisfied customers!' The company launched last month.
body: Testimonials, user counts, and star ratings get inflated, purchased, or algorithmically generated. Fake social proof mimics the appearance of trust.
Numbers are persuasive and easy to fabricate. Verification is rare because trust gets assumed by default.
Take impressive numbers with a grain of salt.
cards.takeaway: Social proof can be manufactured; verification is rare.
